empty dwellings: England – Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of Dwellings) (England) Regulations 
2003 – Class G exception – marketed for sale – appeal dismissed.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel determined that the conditions for Class G exception from the premium for long 
term empty dwellings were not met. The subject property had been marketed for sale for one 
year from 8 June 2023 and therefore, the premium had been correctly applied from 20 March 
2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal challenges the Respondent Billing Authority’s decision of 2 September 2025 in 
respect of the premium for long term empty dwellings, which has been applied to the subject 
property with effect from 20 March 2025.  
 
4. 
The Appellant disagreed with the decision, arguing that the subject property was being 
actively marketed for sale and should therefore be exempt from the premium under Class G. 
The basis for her appeal on 20 September 2025, was that the period that the subject 
property was marketed for sale prior to 1 November 2024 should not be considered by the 
Respondent, as government guidance was not published until that date. 
 
5. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
6. 
The subject property became empty and unfurnished following the vacation of the tenant on 
20 March 2023. As the owner of the property, the Appellant was made liable from that date.  
 
7. 
From 8 June 2023, the Appellant entered into a contract with Richard James Estate Agents 
to sell the subject property on the open market. 
 
8. 
After the subject property had been empty and unfurnished for two years, the Respondent 
applied a premium of 100% to the chargeable amount for council tax from 20 March 2025.  
 
9. 
On 12 March 2025, the Appellant provided the Respondent with evidence to demonstrate 
that the subject property had been actively marketed for sale from 8 June 2023 and, 
consequently, the premium should not be applied. The subject property subsequently sold on 
28 August 2025.  
 
10. In reviewing the evidence provided, the Respondent determined that the Class G exception 
from the higher amount for long term empty dwellings was not applicable on the basis that 
the subject property had been marketed for sale for over twelve months prior to 1 April 2025 
and therefore, the subject property did not meet the requirements set out in legislation. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
11. Part I of the 1992 Act makes provision for billing authorities in England and Wales to levy a 
tax, known as council tax, in respect of domestic hereditaments (“dwellings”) in their 
administrative areas.

12. Section 11(2) of the Act makes provision for a discount in the amount of council tax payable 
in prescribed conditions, including where there is no resident of the dwelling.  So far as is 
relevant, it provides: 
 
11     Discounts 
 
... 
 
(2) 
Subject to sections ... 11B, … below, the amount of council tax payable 
in respect of any chargeable dwelling and any day shall be subject to a 
discount equal to twice the appropriate percentage of that amount if on 
that day— 
 
(a)  there is no resident of the dwelling; or 
 
… 
 
(3) 
In this Section … “the appropriate percentage” means 25 per cent or, if 
the Secretary of State by order so provides in relation to the financial 
year in which the day falls, such other percentage as is specified in the 
order. 
 
13. The discount provided for by section 11(2) of the Act is subject to provisions made in 
section 11B of the Act relating to the imposition of premiums. 
 
14. Section 11B of the Act provides billing authorities with a power to implement a premium in 
the amount of council tax payable for dwellings that are deemed as long-term empty. So far 
as is relevant, it provides: 
 
11B Higher amount for long-term empty dwellings: England 
 
(1) 
For any financial year, a billing authority in England may by 
determination provide in relation to its area, or such part of its area as it 
may specify in the determination, that if on any day a dwelling is a long-
term empty dwelling— 
 
(a) 
the discount under section 11(2)(a) shall not apply, and 
 
(b) 
the amount of council tax payable in respect of that dwelling 
and that day (“the relevant day”) shall be increased by such 
percentage of not more than the relevant maximum) as it 
may so specify. 
 
(1A)  For the financial year beginning on 1 April 2019 the “relevant maximum” 
is 100. 
 
(1B)  For the financial year beginning on 1 April 2020 the “relevant maximum” 
is— 
(a) 
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is less than 5 
years, 100;

www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
(b) 
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 5 years, 
200. 
 
(1C)  For financial years beginning on or after 1 April 2021 the “relevant 
maximum” is— 
 
(a) 
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is less than 5 
years, 100; 
 
(b) 
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 5 years 
but less than 10 years, 200; 
 
(c) 
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 10 
years, 300. 
 
(1D)  In exercising its functions under this section a billing authority must 
have regard to any guidance issued by the Secretary of State. 
 
(2) 
The Secretary of State may by regulations prescribe one or more 
classes of dwelling in relation to which a billing authority may not make 
a determination under this section. 
 
(3) 
A class of dwellings may be prescribed under subsection (2) by 
reference to such factors as the Secretary of State thinks fit and may, in 
particular, be prescribed by reference to— 
 
(a) 
the physical characteristics of, or other matters relating to, 
dwellings; 
 
(b) 
the circumstances of, or other matters relating to, any person 
who is liable to the amount of council tax concerned. 
 
(4) 
Where a determination under this section has effect in relation to a 
class of dwellings— 
 
(a) 
the billing authority may not make a determination under 
section 11A(3), (4) or (4A) in relation to that class, and 
 
(b) 
any determination that has been made under section 11A(3), 
(4) or (4A) ceases to have effect in relation to that class. 
 
(5) 
A billing authority may make a determination varying or revoking a 
determination under this section for a financial year, but only before the 
beginning of the year. 
 
(6) 
A billing authority which makes a determination under this section must 
publish a notice of it in at least one newspaper circulating in its area 

[2026] VTE VT00032183 (CTL)

5/9 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
and do so before the end of the period of 21 days beginning with the 
date of the determination. 
 
(7) 
Failure to comply with subsection (6) does not affect the validity of a 
determination. 
 
(8) 
For the purposes of this section, a dwelling is a “long-term empty 
dwelling” on any day if for a continuous period of at least 1 year ending 
with that day— 
 
(a) 
it has been unoccupied, and 
 
(b) 
it has been substantially unfurnished. 
 
(9) 
In determining whether a dwelling is a long-term empty dwelling, no 
account is to be taken of any one or more periods of not more than 6 
weeks during which either of the conditions in subsection (8)(a) and (b) 
is not met (or neither of them is met). 
 
(10) The Secretary of State may by regulations substitute a different period, 
of not less than 6 weeks, for the period which is for the time being 
specified in subsection (9). 
 
15. The Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 (“the 2023 Act”) changed the definition of a 
long-term empty dwelling from a property that had been unoccupied and substantially 
furnished for two years to one year, provided that the requirements for Section 11B had been 
met. In this case, the Respondent Billing Authority decided not to amend the definition of a 
long-term empty dwelling under its own local scheme. On 21 February 2021, the Respondent 
made a determination for a premium of 100% to be applied to the chargeable amount for 
council tax on any property that had been unoccupied and unfurnished for two years. 
 
16. The regulations referred to in Section 11D(1) are the Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of 
Dwellings) (England) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/3011), where seven new classes have been 
inserted. These Regulations prescribe the classes of dwelling in relation to which a billing 
authority may not make a determination to apply a higher amount of council tax (referred to 
as ‘exceptions’). Relevant to this appeal:  
 
3 Prescribed classes 
 
… 
 
(4) 
Class G, Class H and Class I are prescribed as classes of dwelling for 
the purposes of sections 11B(2) and 11D(1) of the Act for each financial 
year beginning on or after 1st April 2025. 
… 
 
11 Class G 
 
(1) 
The class of dwellings described in this regulation (“Class G”) 
comprises every chargeable dwelling in England— 
 

[2026] VTE VT00032183 (CTL) 
 
D1-BA Decision (v2603) 
6/9 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
(a) 
that is being marketed for sale at a price that is reasonable 
for the sale of the dwelling, or 
(b) 
in relation to which an offer to purchase the dwelling has 
been accepted (whether or not the acceptance is subject to 
contract) but the sale has not been completed, 
 
unless it has been such a dwelling for a period of one year or more. 
 
(2) 
After the end of an excepted period a dwelling does not fall within Class 
G for a further period unless the dwelling has been the subject of a 
relevant transaction. 
 
(3) 
For the purposes of this regulation— 
 
(a) 
marketing a dwelling for sale means the marketing for sale 
of— 
 
(1) the freehold; or 
(2) a leasehold for a term of seven years or more; 
 
(b) 
“excepted period” is a period during which a dwelling falls 
within Class G. 
 
Discussion 
 
17. The issue for the panel to decide in this case was whether the Respondent Billing Authority 
was correct not to award the Class G exception for the period between 20 March 2025 and 
28 August 2025. There had been no disagreement between the parties that the Appellant 
was the owner of the subject property. Additionally, both parties accepted that the subject 
property was empty and unfurnished from 20 March 2023. The dispute, therefore, concerned 
whether the Respondent’s interpretation of the amendments to the legislation that took effect 
the financial year beginning on 1 April 2025 was correct. 
 
18. When considering the case, the panel focused on whether the subject property met the 
criteria for properties actively marketed for sale as set out in legislation. If it was determined 
that the requirements for the criteria had been met, then the exception for dwellings marketed 
for sale could be applied to the chargeable amount for the subject property. In coming to a 
decision on the appeal, the panel considered that the criteria relevant to this case were: 
 
(a) 
that is being marketed for sale at a price that is reasonable for the sale 
of the dwelling,  
… 
unless it has been such a dwelling for a period of one year or more. 
 
19. In analysing the evidence before it, the panel identified that an email from Richard James 
Estate Agents had been provided by the Appellant to the Respondent, along with the link to 
the advertisement for the property on RightMove. In the email dated 20 March 2025, the 
panel confirmed that the property had been marketed for sale on the open market from 8 
June 2023. Per the advertisement on RightMove, the property had initially been marketed for 
sale at £270,000 and had been reduced to £240,000. Additionally, in her bundle, the 
Appellant advised the panel that she had accepted an offer for the property for £238,000 on 
23 April 2025, with a completion date of 28 August 2025. Accordingly, the panel was satisfied 

[2026] VTE VT00032183 (CTL)

that the subject property had been actively marketed for sale for the period between 8 June 
2023 and 28 August 2025. 
 
20. The panel noted the Appellant’s argument that Government guidance on the exceptions 
classes had not been published until 1 November 2024. As such, the Appellant argued this 
was the first date that the subject property should be considered as having been marketed 
for sale. However, the panel considered this interpretation to be incorrect.  The panel had 
regard to regulation 3 of the Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of Dwellings) (England) 
Regulations 2003, which provides that the Class G exception to the council tax premium 
could only take effect from 1 April 2025. Accordingly, the panel found that, although 
Government guidance was published on 1 November 2024, the prescribed Class G 
exception itself did not come into force until 1 April 2025. Therefore, the only period that the 
exception could apply, provided the requirements were met, would from 1 April 2025 until the 
property was sold. 
 
21. In presenting her case to the panel, the Appellant argued that the above Government 
guidance was not issued until 1 November 2024. Therefore, any period that the property was 
marketed for sale prior to that date should not be considered, when applying the exception to 
the chargeable amount for council tax. The Appellant submitted that the purpose of the 
guidance was to avoid penalising owners who were actively seeking to bring properties back 
into use and argued that it was unfair for the exception period to be exhausted before the 
start of the financial year in which the premium became payable. In addition, the Appellant 
advised the panel that she had been informed on four separate occasions by the 
Respondent that the premium would not apply to the chargeable amount of council tax for 
the subject property. The Appellant argued that she had relied upon this advice and had a 
reasonable expectation that the premium would not be imposed. 
 
22. In response to the appeal and presentations to the panel, the Respondent’s representative 
disputed the Appellant’s interpretation of the legislation. It took a literal interpretation of the 
wording of the legislation and argued to the panel that it was clear and deliberate. The billing 
authority’s stance was that the exception could only be considered for one year and did not 
exclude the period prior to the legislation coming into force. In her presentation to the panel, 
the Respondent’s representative advised that the Appellant had been encouraged to apply 
for a Section 13A (1) (c) discretionary discount under its local scheme but, as of the hearing, 
no application had been received. Accordingly, the Respondent’s representative argued that 
it was correct in determining that the Class G exception could not be applied at any point 
during the period in dispute. 
 
23. Having considered the submissions of both parties, the panel determined that the availability 
of the Class G exception from 1 April 2025 did not automatically entitle a property to relief if it 
had currently been on the market for sale. To qualify, the property had to satisfy the statutory 
criteria for the exception. The panel found that the subject property had been actively 
marketed for sale for more than twelve months before 1 April 2025 and therefore did not 
qualify for any period of exemption under Class G. While the panel accepted that the 
Respondent Billing Authority had previously advised the Appellant that the premium would be 
removed, the panel found that the Respondent had erred in its previous claims and, as such, 
were entitled to correct the chargeable amount for council tax for the Appellant in line with 
legislation. As the property had been unoccupied since 20 March 2023, the premium under 
section 11B became payable on 20 March 2025, two years after the property became 
unoccupied and unfurnished.

8/9

24. The Appellant submitted that the Respondent had not provided prior notification that the 
premium for long-term empty dwellings would be applied to her council tax account. Under 
questioning, the Respondent’s representative confirmed that notice of the premium had not 
been published in a local newspaper following the determination made on 21 February 2021, 
as required by section 11B(6) of the Act. However, the representative stated that details of 
the determination had been made available on the Council’s website. In considering this 
issue, the panel found that, under section 11B(7) of the Act, a failure to comply with 
subsection (6) does not affect the validity of the determination. Accordingly, the panel 
concluded that the Respondent’s failure to publish the notice in a local newspaper did not 
invalidate the decision to impose the premium. The panel therefore found that the premium 
had been lawfully applied and that the absence of newspaper publication did not provide 
grounds for allowing the appeal. 
 
25. The panel accepted that the Appellant found it unfair for the period of sale to be considered 
prior to 1 April 2025, however, perceived unfairness arising from the policy choice to apply a 
premium of 100% for council tax on long-term empty dwellings was a matter for Parliament, 
not for this Tribunal. The panel’s role in this case was limited to applying the law as enacted. 
 
26. Accordingly, the panel found that the Respondent could only apply an exception from 1 April 
2025, but the length of the exception was governed by when the property was first marketed, 
not by when the revised legislation would take effect. 
 
Conclusion 
 
27. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the Class G 
exception could not be applied prior to 1 April 2025 and the requirements for the Class G 
exception were not met after 1 April 2025. 
 
28. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
29. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. Any appeal must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 
(Appellant's Notice) within four weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons 
was issued. A party does not require permission from the Tribunal to appeal. 
 
30. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
